terms.definition: Federal Open Market Committee — the Fed's rate-setting body; meets 8 times a year.
European Central Bank — sets rates for the eurozone.
Bank of England — the UK's central bank.
Bank of Japan — Japan's central bank.
Swiss National Bank — Switzerland's central bank.
Reserve Bank of Australia — Australia's central bank.
Bank of Canada — Canada's central bank.
Reserve Bank of New Zealand — NZ's central bank.
Consumer Price Index — the main inflation gauge; measures what households pay.
Personal Consumption Expenditures — the Fed's preferred inflation measure.
Non-Farm Payrolls — the monthly US jobs report; the most watched labor print.
Purchasing Managers' Index — a survey of business activity; above 50 means expansion.
Gross Domestic Product — the total value of an economy's output.
Commitments of Traders — weekly CFTC report showing how speculators are positioned.
Favoring higher interest rates to fight inflation.
Favoring lower rates or looser policy to support growth.
Hundredths of a percent — 25bp = 0.25%. How rate moves are measured.
The return on a bond. Rising yields usually mean tighter financial conditions.
The gap between two yields or rates — e.g. French vs German bonds. Wider = more stress.
Quantitative Tightening — a central bank shrinking its balance sheet; the reverse of QE.
Quantitative Easing — a central bank buying bonds to loosen conditions.
When a central bank buys or sells its own currency to move the exchange rate.
A central bank signaling its future policy intentions to shape expectations.
Monetary Policy Report — a central bank's quarterly outlook on the economy and rates.
French government bonds (Obligations Assimilables du Trésor).
German government bonds — the eurozone's safe-haven benchmark.
Overnight Index Swap — market pricing for where rates are headed.
